title: Claude Tools and Agent Loops
summary: After completing this intermediate module, you can trace a Claude tool interaction, distinguish a predefined workflow from an agent loop, and identify controls that keep repeated tool use bounded and observable.
objectives: Trace how a tool request passes from Claude to an application and how the tool result returns to Claude.
Distinguish a workflow with predefined code paths from an agent that dynamically directs its process and tool use.
Explain how observations from tools influence later decisions in an agent loop.
Select appropriate validation, permission, failure-handling, and stopping controls for repeated tool interactions.

sections.title: Intermediate scope and assumed knowledge
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you understand ordinary application control flow, including requests, responses, validation, and error handling. It does not assume that you know undocumented Claude message fields or configuration keys.

A tool is an operation that an application makes available to Claude through a description. Tool use does not mean that a model request independently executes arbitrary application code. The application remains responsible for deciding what operations are available and for executing client-side operations.

sections.title: Trace a tool interaction
paragraphs: A tool interaction begins when an application supplies Claude with descriptions of available tools. Claude can then produce a request to use an appropriate tool. The application inspects that request, validates its inputs, applies its permission rules, and decides whether to execute the operation.

After execution, the application returns the result to Claude as additional context. Claude can use that observation to produce an answer or to decide that another permitted action is needed. A request, an application-side action, and a returned observation are separate stages, so each can be logged, validated, or rejected independently.
Exact message field names and API structures are intentionally omitted here. They must be taken from the currently resolved Anthropic documentation rather than inferred from this conceptual sequence.
sections.callout: Treat model output as a request for an application-controlled action, not as proof that the action has already occurred.

sections.title: Distinguish workflows from agents
paragraphs: In a workflow, model and tool calls follow paths predefined by application code. The application determines the sequence, even when a model contributes content or classifications within that sequence.

In an agent, the model dynamically directs more of the process and tool usage. It evaluates available context, selects or requests an action, observes the result, and decides whether to continue. The returned observation can change the next decision, which is why an agent loop is more than a fixed sequence of calls.

Agentic behavior is not automatically preferable. Use the simplest architecture that satisfies the task. A predictable process with known steps is often better represented as a workflow, while a task that requires decisions based on changing observations may justify a bounded agent loop.

sections.title: Bound and supervise the loop
paragraphs: An agent loop needs explicit completion criteria and stopping conditions. Without them, repeated model and tool interactions can continue after useful progress has stopped. An implementation can limit iterations, stop after completion, halt on repeated failures, or require human approval before sensitive operations.

Tool inputs should be validated before execution. Permissions should restrict which operations and resources are available. Failures should be returned in a form that lets the system stop safely or choose an allowed recovery path. Logs should preserve requests, decisions, results, and termination reasons so that behavior can be reviewed.
These controls belong around the model interaction. The application, not the model alone, enforces permissions, iteration limits, and execution policy.

questions.prompt: Claude returns a request to use a client-side tool. What happens next according to this module?
choices: The request proves that the operation has already executed.
The application validates the request, applies permissions, and decides whether to execute it.
Claude automatically grants the tool access to every application resource.
The agent loop must terminate before the application can inspect the request.
questions.explanation: The application controls client-side execution. It inspects and validates the request, enforces permissions, and then decides whether to perform the operation.

questions.prompt: Which description best distinguishes a workflow from an agent?
choices: A workflow follows predefined code paths, while an agent dynamically directs more of its process and tool use.
A workflow always uses tools, while an agent never uses tools.
A workflow has no application code, while an agent is entirely predefined.
A workflow cannot process results, while an agent cannot stop.
questions.explanation: The module defines workflows by predefined orchestration paths and agents by dynamic decisions informed by context and observations.

questions.prompt: Why is a returned tool result important in an agent loop?
choices: It removes the need for input validation.
It grants the model permanent execution permission.
It supplies an observation that can inform the next decision.
It guarantees that another tool must be requested.
questions.explanation: A tool result becomes an observation available to Claude. That observation can affect whether the loop continues, changes direction, or stops.

questions.prompt: Which control directly prevents an agent loop from continuing indefinitely?
choices: Using an explicit iteration limit or stopping condition
Treating each tool request as already executed
questions.explanation: An explicit iteration limit or other stopping condition bounds the number of repeated model and tool interactions.
